title: Tiredness, steatorrhoea and an itchy rash on the knees in a 28-year-old lawyer
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 28-year-old lawyer with two months of tiredness, abdominal pain, pale foul-smelling diarrhoea, weight loss and an itchy rash on both knees. The candidate then interprets a photograph of the rash and her blood and stool results, and plans the coeliac disease work-up and management, safety netting and follow-up in general practice.
focus: Fatigue with malabsorption: recognising coeliac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis and iron deficiency, interpreting coeliac serology, and keeping the patient on gluten until biopsy in general practice
stem: You are a GP registrar in a city general practice. Rachel Zane, a 28-year-old lawyer, has come to see you because she has been feeling exceptionally tired for the past 2 months. A practice nurse is available to chaperone.
tasks: Take a focused history from Rachel and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you a photograph of the rash on Rachel's knees and the results of her blood and stool tests. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Rachel Zane, a 28-year-old lawyer at a busy city firm. You are articulate, a little impatient, and inclined to blame your job for everything. You give the facts below only when asked about them. You agree to be examined. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I've been feeling very tired recently."

The tiredness (give only when asked):

  • You have been exceptionally tired at work for 2 months. You struggle to get through the afternoon.
  • You sleep about 6 hours a night and work long hours, but that has always been the case: no change in your routine.
  • Your diet is normal. You are not vegetarian and have eaten nothing unusual.

Tummy and bowels (give only when asked):

  • Pain: crampy pain around the belly button. Only if asked what makes it worse: it is worse after meals. Only if asked: it does not go through to your back.
  • Diarrhoea: a lot of it. Only if asked to describe the stool: loose, foul-smelling and pale.
  • You burp a lot and feel bloated.
  • Weight: you have lost 3 kg in the past month without trying (from about 59 kg).
  • No nausea, vomiting or blood in the stool. Nobody has said you look yellow.

Skin (only if asked about rashes or the skin): for about a month you have had a rash on both knees. It is very itchy and you keep scratching it. You thought it was your old eczema coming back and have been putting moisturiser on it, which has not helped.

Periods (only if asked): your periods have always been heavy; the pill made them a bit lighter, but they are still heavy, regular, and no worse recently. You are on the pill.

Other systems (all negative if asked): no snoring or falling asleep in the day; no shortness of breath, cough or chest pain; no change in hair or in how you cope with heat or cold; not passing more urine or more thirsty than usual; you have not noticed looking pale; no bruising and no night sweats; no joint pain. Your mood is good. Work is stressful, but nothing new.

Past medical history: eczema, allergic asthma and hay fever since childhood, but none of them has been a problem for 15 years. Never been in hospital. Immunisations up to date.

Medicines: the oral contraceptive pill for 3 years; you cannot remember which one. Nothing else, no supplements. Allergies: none known.

Family history: your mother has Graves' disease. Your father is well. Your twin brother was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes 2 years ago.

Social history:

  • Social smoker: 1 or 2 cigarettes a month.
  • Alcohol: you drink with clients and keep up with whatever they drink, so it is unpredictable. If pressed for numbers: some weeks nothing, some weeks two or three client dinners with several glasses of wine. You never drink alone.
  • No recreational drugs.
  • You live with your partner in an apartment and have good support.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Idea: you think you are probably burnt out from work.
  • Concern: you are in the middle of a big case and cannot afford to be off sick.
  • Expectation: some blood tests, and something to give you more energy.

Question to raise near the end of Part 1: "Could this all just be stress?"

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they examine):

  • General: slim, tired-looking, comfortable at rest, alert.
  • Observations: BP 112/70 mmHg, HR 88/min regular, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C. Weight 56 kg, height 167 cm, BMI 20 kg/m2. Capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L (random). Pregnancy test, if asked: a serum beta-hCG is sent with the bloods; the result is given in Part 2.
  • Hands: no koilonychia, clubbing, tremor or palmar erythema.
  • Face and mouth: mild conjunctival pallor. Angular cheilitis at both corners of the mouth. Tongue normal. No mouth ulcers. No jaundice.
  • Neck and eyes: thyroid not enlarged, no nodules or bruit. No lid lag or exophthalmos. No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
  • Heart and chest: normal heart sounds, no murmurs; chest clear.
  • Abdomen: mildly distended, soft. Mild periumbilical tenderness without guarding. No masses, no hepatosplenomegaly. Bowel sounds active. No scars. Rectal examination: "Not needed today."
  • Skin: on the extensor surfaces of both knees, symmetrical clusters of small blisters and scratched, crusted bumps on a red background. Elbows, buttocks and scalp clear. Elbow and knee creases (flexures) clear, with no dry, thickened skin. No bruising. (A photograph of the knees is handed over in Part 2.)

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Rachel's identity and explains the purpose of the consultation.
Uses plain language, takes her symptoms seriously rather than accepting 'just stress', and acknowledges her worry about her work.
Gains consent for the examination, and offers a chaperone, particularly before inspecting the buttocks.
History
Characterises the tiredness: 2 months, at work, sleeps 6 hours, long hours but no change in routine, normal diet and not vegetarian.
Takes a gastrointestinal history:

kids.x: Abdominal pain: crampy, periumbilical, worse after meals, not radiating to the back.
Describes the stool: loose, pale and foul-smelling (steatorrhoea).
Quantifies the weight loss: 3 kg in a month, unintentional.
Red-flag negatives: no blood in the stool, vomiting, nausea or jaundice.

check.x: Asks about the skin and finds the itchy rash on both knees for a month, which she thought was eczema and has been moisturising.
Takes a menstrual history and considers pregnancy: always heavy periods, a bit lighter on the pill but still heavy, regular, on the OCP.
Screens the other systems for causes of fatigue:
check.d: Award for clusters from each system; the negatives are listed in the script.

kids.x: Thyroid and diabetes: heat or cold intolerance, hair change, polyuria, polydipsia [none].
Sleep and cardiorespiratory: snoring, daytime sleepiness, breathlessness, cough, chest pain [none].
Constitutional and haematological: night sweats, bruising, pallor, joint pain [none].
Mood and stress [mood good, work stressful but nothing new].

check.x: Takes the past medical history: childhood eczema, allergic asthma and hay fever, quiet for 15 years; no admissions; immunisations up to date.
Takes a medication and allergy history: OCP for 3 years (type unknown), nothing else, no known allergies.
Takes a family history and identifies the autoimmune pattern: mother with Graves' disease, twin brother with type 1 diabetes diagnosed 2 years ago.

Takes a social history: smoking (1 to 2 a month), alcohol quantified as far as possible (unpredictable, with clients, not alone), no drugs, lives with her partner, good support, works long hours as a lawyer.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is burnout, worried about her big case, expects blood tests and something for energy.
Examination
Asks for observations, weight and BMI, and compares the weight with before [BP 112/70, HR 88, afebrile, 56 kg, BMI 20, down 3 kg].
Looks for signs of anaemia and nutritional deficiency in the hands, eyes and mouth [mild conjunctival pallor, angular cheilitis, no koilonychia].
Examines the thyroid and looks for thyroid eye signs and tremor [normal].
Examines the abdomen including lymph nodes and organomegaly [mild distension and periumbilical tenderness, no masses, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy].
Examines the rash and the other typical sites: both knees, elbows, buttocks, scalp and the flexures [grouped blisters and excoriated papules on both knees; elsewhere clear].
Interpretation

Photograph: describes symmetrical grouped vesicles and excoriated, crusted papules on the extensor knees, and gives dermatitis herpetiformis as most likely with atopic dermatitis (eczema) as the alternative, noting the extensor rather than flexural site.
FBC and iron studies: Hb 104 g/L with MCV 74 and ferritin 6 is microcytic iron deficiency anaemia, attributed to both malabsorption and heavy periods.

Coeliac serology: tTG-IgA 128 U/mL (more than 10 times the upper limit) with a normal total IgA, so the result is valid, plus a positive DGP-IgG: highly suggestive of coeliac disease, to be confirmed by duodenal biopsy.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 is not needed because the serology is not equivocal.

check.x: Identifies other evidence of malabsorption: low folate, low vitamin D (32 nmol/L), albumin 34 g/L and a mildly raised ALT, which is common in coeliac disease.
Notes the reassuring negatives: normal TSH and free T4, negative beta-hCG, normal CRP and ESR, normal B12.
Stool: no pathogens or parasites, so infection (including Giardia) is unlikely; fat globules confirm steatorrhoea; normal faecal elastase makes pancreatic insufficiency unlikely.
States the most likely diagnosis as coeliac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis, complicated by iron deficiency anaemia and folate and vitamin D deficiency.

Names at least three differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case, for example: small-bowel Crohn's disease, iron deficiency from heavy periods alone, chronic pancreatitis, hyperthyroidism, Giardia or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, atopic dermatitis.
check.d: Credit any other sensible differential argued from this case's features.

check.x: Management
Tells Rachel to keep eating gluten until the biopsy, because stopping it first can make the biopsy and serology falsely normal.
Refers to gastroenterology for gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies to confirm the diagnosis.
Replaces the deficiencies:

kids.x: Oral iron (about 100 mg elemental iron daily or on alternate days), with IV iron if not tolerated or not absorbed.
Folic acid 5 mg orally daily for about 4 months, after confirming B12 is normal.
Vitamin D: cholecalciferol 1000 to 2000 units orally daily (mild deficiency), rechecked at about 3 months.

check.x: Plans, once confirmed, a lifelong strict gluten-free diet with an accredited practising dietitian and Coeliac Australia support.
Explains that the rash settles slowly on a gluten-free diet and refers to dermatology if it is severe.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: dapsone in the interim (G6PD first, blood count monitoring); perilesional skin biopsy for direct immunofluorescence.

check.x: Recommends coeliac screening for her first-degree relatives, especially her twin brother with type 1 diabetes, if not tested recently, and plans to review her heavy periods if they persist once iron is replaced.
Arranges follow-up: review after the gastroscopy, a repeat FBC and iron studies to check the response to iron, and a repeat tTG-IgA after 6 to 12 months on the diet.
check.d: Exact intervals are credit, not required.

check.x: Safety netting

Explains in plain language that coeliac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that damages the small bowel and stops it absorbing iron and vitamins, that it is common and treatable, and checks understanding.

Gives specific red flags in plain words: black or bloody stools, persistent vomiting, severe or worsening abdominal pain, chest pain, breathlessness or fainting, or very heavy bleeding need urgent review (ED, or 000 if collapsing); see the GP sooner if diarrhoea or weight loss worsens, the rash spreads or she cannot tolerate iron.
check.d: Award for at least three specific urgent red flags (for example black or bloody stools, persistent vomiting, fainting or breathlessness) with where to go, plus at least one see-the-GP-sooner trigger. Vague advice such as 'come back if worse' does not score.

part2.lead: A week later, Rachel's results are back. Here is the photograph of her knees taken at the first visit, and the results of her blood and stool tests.
part2.patient:
Rachel is not part of Questions 1 to 3. During Question 4 she asks:

  • "So should I stop eating bread straight away?" (Surprised to hear she should keep eating gluten until the biopsy.)
  • "Is this serious? Can I keep working on my case?"

handover.label: Clinical photograph: both knees
handover.result:
Clinical photograph, taken at the first visit with consent. Anterior view of both knees.

  • On the extensor surfaces of both knees, symmetrical clusters of small (2 to 4 mm) tense vesicles, grouped in a herpetiform pattern.
  • Many lesions are excoriated, with erosions, crusts and small red papules; a background of mild erythema.
  • No lichenification, scale or thickened skin. No pustules or honey-coloured crusting.
  • Popliteal fossae (knee creases) clear.
handover.model:
Read: symmetrical, grouped small vesicles and excoriated, crusted papules on the extensor surfaces of both knees, with the flexures spared and no lichenification.

For Rachel: an intensely itchy, symmetrical, vesicular rash on the extensor surfaces is typical of dermatitis herpetiformis, the skin form of coeliac disease. Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is the alternative given her childhood eczema, but adult eczema is usually flexural with dry, thickened (lichenified) skin, and it has not responded to moisturiser.

What it changes: it strongly supports coeliac disease. It settles on a gluten-free diet; dermatology review if severe (dapsone), and a perilesional skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence can confirm it.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.result: Collected at 08:30. Blood film: hypochromic microcytic red cells with pencil cells, consistent with iron deficiency.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 104 g/L, MCV 74, MCH 23, high RDW, mild thrombocytosis; ferritin 6, low iron and transferrin saturation, high transferrin: iron deficiency anaemia. Folate low, B12 normal. Vitamin D 32 nmol/L (deficient). Albumin 34 and ALT 48 mildly abnormal. tTG-IgA 128 U/mL with normal total IgA, DGP-IgG 86. TSH, free T4, CRP, ESR, electrolytes and glucose normal. Beta-hCG negative.
  • For Rachel: serology this high (about 18 times the upper limit) with a normal IgA is highly suggestive of coeliac disease. Iron and folate (absorbed in the proximal small bowel) and vitamin D are low from malabsorption, and her heavy periods add to the iron loss. The mild ALT rise is common in coeliac disease. Normal thyroid function is against hyperthyroidism, normal CRP and ESR make active IBD less likely but do not exclude small-bowel Crohn's, and she is not pregnant.
  • What it changes: gastroscopy with duodenal biopsy while she still eats gluten; replace iron, folate and vitamin D; screen first-degree relatives.

labs.title: Full blood count and iron studies

handover.label: Stool tests
handover.result:
Faeces: microscopy, culture, multiplex PCR and faecal elastase. Specimen: loose, pale stool, collected 5 days ago.

  • Microscopy: numerous fat globules seen. No red cells; scanty white cells. No ova, cysts or parasites.
  • Culture: Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter and Yersinia not isolated.
  • Multiplex PCR: Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba histolytica, Clostridioides difficile toxin and enteric viruses not detected.
  • Faecal elastase: 410 microgram/g (normal above 200).

Conclusion: no enteric pathogen detected. Increased faecal fat. Faecal elastase normal: exocrine pancreatic insufficiency unlikely.
handover.model:
Read: no bacterial, parasitic or viral pathogen, including Giardia; increased fat globules; faecal elastase normal at 410.

For Rachel: the fat confirms the steatorrhoea she describes. A normal elastase makes pancreatic insufficiency (and so chronic pancreatitis causing malabsorption) unlikely despite her unpredictable drinking, and infection, including Giardia, is very unlikely as the cause of 2 months of diarrhoea. The malabsorption is therefore from the small bowel, fitting coeliac disease.

What it changes: no antimicrobial treatment and no pancreatic imaging or enzyme replacement; proceed to gastroscopy and duodenal biopsy.

ask: You are now calling the gastroenterology registrar to arrange a gastroscopy. Please give an ISBAR handover of Rachel Zane, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Rachel now, here in general practice.
Rachel is back in the room. Explain the results to her, answer her questions, and tell her what to look out for.
expect:
• Identify: self, GP registrar; Rachel Zane, 28-year-old lawyer.
  • Situation: probable coeliac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis; requesting gastroscopy with duodenal biopsy.
  • Background: 2 months of fatigue, periumbilical pain after meals, pale foul-smelling diarrhoea, bloating, 3 kg weight loss, itchy rash on both knees. Lifelong heavy periods, on the OCP. Mother Graves' disease, twin brother type 1 diabetes.
  • Assessment: grouped vesicles on the extensor knees, likely dermatitis herpetiformis. tTG-IgA 128 (over 10 times normal) with normal total IgA, DGP-IgG positive. Hb 104, MCV 74, ferritin 6: iron deficiency anaemia. Low folate and vitamin D, albumin 34, ALT 48. TFTs, CRP and ESR normal; beta-hCG negative. Stool: no pathogens, fat globules, normal elastase.
  • Recommendation: gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies; she is still eating gluten. I am replacing iron, folate and vitamin D.

Any three argued from the case score; the list below is for examiner reference.

Most likely: coeliac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis, with iron, folate and vitamin D deficiency. For: steatorrhoea, bloating, weight loss, typical rash, autoimmune family history, tTG-IgA over 10 times normal with normal IgA.

  • Crohn's disease (small bowel): for: periumbilical pain, weight loss, iron and folate deficiency, low albumin. Against: no blood or mucus, no mouth ulcers, normal CRP and ESR, serology strongly positive for coeliac. If duodenal histology is not typical: faecal calprotectin, or ileocolonoscopy (with terminal ileal biopsy), with MR enterography or capsule endoscopy if needed.
  • Iron deficiency from heavy periods alone: for: lifelong heavy periods. Against: does not explain diarrhoea, weight loss, low folate or serology.
  • Chronic pancreatitis: for: steatorrhoea, alcohol. Against: normal faecal elastase.
  • Hyperthyroidism (Graves'): for: mother, weight loss, diarrhoea. Against: no tremor or goitre, normal TFTs.
  • Atopic dermatitis (rash): for: childhood eczema. Against: extensor, vesicular, flexures spared.

1. Keep eating gluten until the biopsy; do not start a gluten-free diet yet.
  2. Refer to gastroenterology for gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies.
  3. Replace deficiencies: oral iron about 100 mg elemental iron daily or on alternate days (IV iron if not tolerated or not absorbed); folic acid 5 mg orally daily for about 4 months (B12 normal); cholecalciferol 1000 to 2000 units orally daily, recheck at about 3 months.
  4. Once confirmed: lifelong strict gluten-free diet, accredited practising dietitian, Coeliac Australia.
  5. Rash: settles slowly on the diet; dermatology if severe.
  6. Family: coeliac serology for first-degree relatives, especially her twin if not tested recently. Review heavy periods if they persist.
  7. Follow-up: after gastroscopy; recheck FBC and iron; tTG-IgA 6 to 12 months on the diet.

• In plain words: probably coeliac disease, an immune reaction to gluten; common, treatable with diet; she can keep working.
  • Keep eating gluten (e.g. bread daily) until the biopsy, or the test can be falsely normal.
  • Go to ED (000 if collapsing): black or bloody stools, persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, chest pain, breathlessness, fainting, very heavy bleeding.
  • See the GP sooner: worsening diarrhoea or weight loss, spreading rash, cannot tolerate iron.

ddx.for: Pale foul-smelling diarrhoea, bloating, 3 kg weight loss, grouped vesicles on both extensor knees, a mother with Graves' and a twin with type 1 diabetes, and tTG-IgA 128 U/mL with normal total IgA.
Periumbilical pain, weight loss, iron and folate deficiency, and a low albumin.
ddx.against: No blood or mucus, no mouth ulcers, normal CRP and ESR, and serology strongly positive for coeliac; faecal calprotectin, or ileocolonoscopy (with terminal ileal biopsy), with MR enterography or capsule endoscopy if needed, if duodenal histology is not typical.

ddx.dx: Iron deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding alone
ddx.for: She has always had heavy periods and has a ferritin of 6 with a microcytic anaemia.
ddx.against: Heavy periods do not explain the steatorrhoea, weight loss, low folate and vitamin D, or the strongly positive coeliac serology.

ddx.dx: Chronic pancreatitis with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
ddx.for: She has pale, foul-smelling stools with fat globules and unpredictable, at times heavy, drinking.
ddx.against: Her faecal elastase is normal at 410 and her pain does not radiate to the back.

ddx.for: Her mother has Graves' disease and she has fatigue, weight loss and diarrhoea.
ddx.against: She has no heat intolerance, tremor, goitre or eye signs, and her TSH and free T4 are normal.

ddx.for: She had eczema as a child and thought the rash was eczema.
ddx.against: The rash is vesicular and on the extensor surfaces, the flexures are spared, there is no lichenification, and moisturiser has not helped.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Rachel mentions the rash only if asked about her skin, describes her stool only if asked what it looks like, and says the pain is worse after meals only if asked. Full marks for the systems review need clusters from each system, not one question each.

In Part 2 hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Questions 1 to 3 are a discussion with the registrar and examiner, so Rachel stays silent; for Question 4 she is back in the room and the person playing her puts her questions. The rash differentials (dermatitis herpetiformis versus atopic dermatitis) are earned when the candidate reads the photograph.

A high-performing candidate refuses to settle for "stress", finds the steatorrhoea, weight loss, rash, heavy periods and autoimmune family history, and examines the skin at the typical extensor sites. In Part 2 they check total IgA before trusting the tTG, link the iron deficiency to both malabsorption and menstruation, use the normal elastase and TFTs to argue against the differentials, and clearly tell Rachel to keep eating gluten until the biopsy.

A borderline candidate takes a generic fatigue screen, misses the rash or calls it eczema, interprets the tTG without total IgA, starts a gluten-free diet before the biopsy, or gives vague safety netting.
explain:
Approach to fatigue

Fatigue is common and often attributed to lifestyle, but a new, persistent change with physical symptoms needs a structured search. Screen by system:

  • sleep (duration, sleep apnoea);
  • anaemia and blood loss (periods, gastrointestinal);
  • endocrine (thyroid, diabetes, pregnancy);
  • gastrointestinal and malabsorption;
  • infection and inflammation (sweats, joints);
  • mood and substance use.

Rachel's sleep and routine have not changed. Her steatorrhoea, weight loss, itchy rash and autoimmune family history point to an organic cause.

Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten in genetically susceptible people (HLA-DQ2 or DQ8). It is common in Australia and often goes undiagnosed. It can present with:

  • diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, bloating, wind and abdominal pain;
  • weight loss and fatigue;
  • iron deficiency, low folate and low vitamin D;
  • a mildly raised ALT;
  • dermatitis herpetiformis.

Risk is higher in first-degree relatives and in people with other autoimmune disease, especially type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease. Rachel's mother has Graves' disease and her twin brother has type 1 diabetes.

Dermatitis herpetiformis

Dermatitis herpetiformis is an intensely itchy, symmetrical rash. It shows grouped vesicles that are usually excoriated by the time they are seen. It affects the extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees, the buttocks and the scalp. It is specific to coeliac disease. A biopsy of the skin next to a lesion, with direct immunofluorescence, shows granular IgA in the dermal papillae. It responds slowly to a gluten-free diet. Dapsone, from a dermatologist, controls the itch in the meantime; check G6PD and monitor the blood count. Adult atopic dermatitis is usually flexural, with dry, lichenified skin, and is not vesicular.

Interpreting the serology

  • tTG-IgA is the first-line test, but only with a total IgA level. IgA deficiency is more common in coeliac disease and gives a falsely negative tTG-IgA; DGP-IgG or tTG-IgG is then used.
  • Rachel's tTG-IgA is more than 10 times the upper limit (128 against an upper limit of 7, about 18 times) with a normal IgA and a positive DGP-IgG. This is highly suggestive, but in adults the diagnosis is still confirmed by duodenal biopsy.
  • Serology and histology both become normal on a gluten-free diet. The patient must keep eating gluten until the biopsy. If gluten has already been stopped, a supervised gluten challenge is needed first.
  • HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing is useful when results are equivocal or the person is already gluten-free. A negative result effectively excludes coeliac disease. It is not needed here.

The other results

  • Iron deficiency anaemia: microcytic, ferritin 6. Iron is absorbed in the duodenum, the part most affected by coeliac disease, and her heavy periods add to the loss.
  • Low folate and vitamin D also reflect proximal small bowel malabsorption.
  • Stool tests: no infection, including Giardia. Fat globules confirm steatorrhoea. A normal faecal elastase argues against pancreatic insufficiency from chronic pancreatitis.
  • Normal CRP and ESR: make active inflammatory bowel disease less likely but do not exclude small-bowel Crohn's disease, which also causes periumbilical pain, weight loss and iron and folate deficiency. If the duodenal histology is not typical of coeliac disease, check faecal calprotectin or arrange ileocolonoscopy (with terminal ileal biopsy), with MR enterography or capsule endoscopy if needed.
  • Normal TSH and free T4: exclude hyperthyroidism.
  • Negative beta-hCG: excludes pregnancy.
  • Vitamin D deficiency adds to fatigue but does not explain the whole picture.

Management

  • Confirm: refer to gastroenterology for gastroscopy with multiple duodenal biopsies while she is on gluten.
  • Replace deficiencies now:
    • oral iron, about 100 mg elemental iron daily or on alternate days;
    • IV iron if it is not tolerated or not absorbed;
    • folic acid 5 mg orally daily for about 4 months, once B12 is known to be normal;
    • cholecalciferol 1000 to 2000 units orally daily (vitamin D 32 nmol/L, mild deficiency), recheck at about 3 months. Higher doses may be needed while malabsorption persists; recheck 25-OH vitamin D at about 3 months and adjust.
  • Once confirmed:
    • a lifelong strict gluten-free diet, avoiding wheat, rye, barley and, for most, oats;
    • an accredited practising dietitian and Coeliac Australia membership;
    • consider a bone density scan given her low vitamin D.
  • Screening: offer serology to first-degree relatives, especially her twin brother with type 1 diabetes, if not tested recently.
  • Heavy menstrual bleeding: reassess and manage according to the ACSQHC Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Clinical Care Standard if it persists.
  • Lifestyle: brief advice on alcohol and smoking.

Safety netting and follow-up

  • Urgent review (ED, or 000 if collapsing): black or bloody stools, persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, chest pain, breathlessness or fainting (symptomatic anaemia), or very heavy bleeding.
  • Follow-up:
    • review after the gastroscopy;
    • FBC in 2 to 4 weeks to check Hb is rising, and iron studies at about 3 months;
    • tTG-IgA 6 to 12 months after starting the diet, then yearly review of symptoms, diet, blood count, iron, folate, vitamin D, thyroid function and liver tests.
  • Persistent symptoms despite the diet need gastroenterology review. The usual cause is ongoing gluten exposure, but refractory disease and lymphoma are rare causes to consider.
points: Do not accept 'stress' for new fatigue with diarrhoea and weight loss: screen every system, and ask specifically about the stool, the skin and the periods.
Pale, foul-smelling stools with weight loss mean malabsorption. A normal faecal elastase points away from the pancreas and towards the small bowel.
Grouped, excoriated vesicles on the extensor knees, elbows or buttocks are dermatitis herpetiformis, which is specific to coeliac disease.
Always interpret tTG-IgA together with total IgA. If IgA is deficient, use DGP-IgG or tTG-IgG.
Confirm coeliac disease in adults with duodenal biopsy while the patient is still eating gluten. Starting a gluten-free diet first makes the tests falsely normal.

Replace iron, folate and vitamin D, start a lifelong gluten-free diet with a dietitian once the diagnosis is confirmed, and offer serology to first-degree relatives, especially those with type 1 diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease.

imaging.finding: Symmetrical clusters of small tense vesicles with excoriated, crusted papules on the extensor surfaces of both knees, on a background of mild erythema, without lichenification
imaging.caption: Clinical photograph of both knees, taken at the first visit.
imaging.alt: Both knees showing symmetrical clusters of small blisters and scratched, crusted red bumps on the front of the knees.
